L6: # Clinical Study for Cats with Mammary Cancer - Information for referring veterinarians
L7: 
L8: ##
L9: ## Why refer your patients?
L10: 
L11:   * The therapy (GCN2-IN-6) has been carefully tested in preclinical studies and is well-tolerated.
L12:   * Your referred patients will receive standard surgical care plus the investigational therapy.
L13:   * Participation contributes valuable data for advancing cancer treatments in both cats and humans.
L14: ## Study design highlights
L15: 
L16:   * Neo-adjuvant and adjuvant therapy administered around the time of mastectomy.
L17: 
L18:   * Safety and efficacy are continuously monitored.
L19: 
L20:   * Feline mammary adenocarcinoma is a validated model for TNBC research.
L21: ## Referral process
L22: 
L23:   * Eligible cats: cats diagnosed with mammary tumors, eligible for surgery.
L24: 
L25:   * As referring veterinarians, you can retain primary responsibility for routine care; the study team coordinates treatment administration and follow-up.
L26: 
L27:   * Participation is voluntary, and owners can withdraw at any time.
L28: ## Impact:
L29: 
L30: By referring cats to this study, you are helping advance cutting-edge cancer research, improve therapeutic options, and potentially enhance outcomes for both feline and human patients.
L31: ## Contact
L32: 
L33: Further information can be obtained by mailing Ada Krupa (adriana.krupa@ugent.be) or Hilde de Rooster (hilde.derooster@ugent.be) or by phone (+32 9 264 77 00).

L5: # New Patients Welcome: OVC Researchers Evaluating Non-Surgical Treatment for Cats with Oral Cancer
L6: 
L7: Posted on Wednesday, August 28, 2024
L8: Researchers at the Ontario Veterinary College (OVC) are seeking feline patients to participate in a study exploring a minimally invasive treatment for oral cancer. Led by Dr. Michelle Oblak, Animal Health Partners Research Chair in Veterinary Medical Innovation, the research team is evaluating the use of nanoparticles and laser light therapy as a non-surgical treatment approach for cats diagnosed with oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC).
L9: ## About OCSCC
L10: 
L11: OCSCC is a relatively common and aggressive type of oral cancer in cats. It typically originates in the tissues of the mouth, including the gums, tongue and palate and presents as an ulcerative lesion that can cause drooling, bad breath and difficulty eating.
L12: OCSCC often progresses rapidly, invading surrounding tissues and bone within the oral cavity. Although rare, the disease may also spread to lymph nodes and organs. While the exact cause is not fully understood, factors such as chronic inflammation, exposure to carcinogens and viral infections (such as papillomavirus) may contribute to its development.
L13: ## Poor Treatment Prognosis
L14: 
L15: Early detection is an important factor in optimizing treatment outcomes for cats with OCSCC. Treatment approaches vary depending on the tumour size and location, and whether or not the cancer has spread.
L16: 
L17: Sadly, even with treatment, the prognosis for most cats is poor: cats treated with surgery, chemotherapy or radiation typically live for only one to four months. Less than 10 per cent of cats survive for one year after diagnosis.

L3@P0: Diagnosis “glioma” – what now?
L4@P0: Dogs diagnosed with a brain tumor can confront their owners with a variety of symptoms, ranging from
L5@P0: behavioral changes to epileptic seizures. It is often assumed that the tumor is a so-called glioma. This
L6@P0: tumor, which originates in the supporting cells of the brain, is also frequently diagnosed in humans.
L7@P0: Around 75% of affected dogs suffer from an aggressive form – high-grade glioma.
L8@P0: The standard treatment for gliomas in humans is multimodal and consists of surgical removal, radiation
L9@P0: therapy, and chemotherapy. In dogs, however, radiation therapy is the most common form of treatment.
L10@P0: Chemotherapy is still not widely used for brain tumors in dogs.
L11@P0: Based on recent results in humans with gliomas, combined therapy using radiation therapy and
L12@P0: chemotherapy with lomustine and temozolomide can significantly prolong survival without
L13@P0: compromising quality of life. Lomustine and temozolomide are already used to treat other types of
L14@P0: tumors in dogs, and the tolerability of both drugs in dogs has already been investigated. In this study,
L15@P0: we want to investigate whether we can also significantly improve survival time in dogs with high-grade
L16@P0: gliomas without compromising their quality of life.
